blocks.text: STOP DRIVING IMMEDIATELY — THIS IS CRITICAL

If your temperature gauge enters the red zone or you notice steam escaping from the bonnet: Pull over safely immediately. Turn off the engine—do not let it idle. Never open the expansion tank cap while the engine is hot due to the risk of severe steam scalding. Wait 30–60 minutes before inspecting coolant levels.

items.title: Common Causes of Engine Overheating (UK Focus)
items.description: Comprehensive cost, failure mechanics, and vehicle susceptibility breakdown for UK motorists.

rows: Low Coolant Level
Gradual fluid loss from split rubber hose, leaking radiator seam, or water pump seal weep.
All vehicles over 6–8 years old
Thermostat Stuck Closed
Internal wax element fails; thermostat remains shut, trapping boiling coolant inside the engine block.
VW EA189, Ford DV6 1.6 TDCi, BMW N47, Mercedes OM651
Water Pump Failure
Plastic impeller shears off shaft or bearings seize, halting coolant circulation across the radiator.
BMW N47 (plastic impeller), VW EA189, Jaguar AJ126
Cooling Fan / Relay Failure
Electric fan motor, resistor pack, or relay burns out, causing rapid overheating in slow traffic or idle.
Renault K9K 1.5 dCi, Ford Focus Mk3, Vauxhall Astra
Radiator Blockage / Leak
External stone impact damage, corrosion, or internal sediment sludge blocking narrow coolant channels.
High-mileage cars over 10 years old
Blown Head Gasket
Combustion pressure breaches fire ring, pushing boiling exhaust gas directly into the cooling system.
Direct consequence of unaddressed earlier overheating
Critically Low Engine Oil
Engine oil accounts for up to 40% of internal heat dissipation; low level causes extreme friction heat.
Neglected servicing intervals across all models

blocks.text: Market context: Based on 24,650 quote requests in 2025, the most common overheating-related repairs occur on high-mileage diesel engines (VW EA189, BMW N47, Ford DV6, Mercedes OM651). [EM-VERIFIED]

items.title: 7-Step Diagnostic Process: Finding the Root Cause
items.description: A competent specialist will never replace a head gasket without systematically identifying why the engine overheated first.

rows: Coolant Level & Expansion Tank Inspection
Checks for low fluid level, discoloured coolant, or air locks.
Pressurised Leak Detection Test
Pressurises cooling circuit to 1.5 bar to locate weeping hoses or radiator core leaks.
Thermostat Opening Verification
Measures top/bottom radiator hose temperature differential using infrared thermometer.
Electric Cooling Fan Circuit Activation
Commands high-speed fan relay via OBD2 scan tool and tests A/C fan cycling.
Water Pump Flow & Weep Hole Test
Verifies coolant return flow rate into expansion bottle and checks pump shaft play.
Chemical Block Sniffer Test
Draws expansion tank air through chemical reagent; blue turns yellow if CO2 exhaust gas is present.
Cylinder Leak-Down & Compression Test
Quantifies mechanical cylinder pressure loss directly into adjacent coolant jackets.

blocks.text: Specialist Rule of Thumb: 90% of overheating complaints on vehicles over 60,000 miles stem from either a stuck thermostat or a failed water pump impeller. If you are replacing the timing belt or timing chain, always replace both the water pump and thermostat simultaneously—the labour overlap saves hundreds of pounds.

items.title: Repair vs Replace: What Should You Do?
items.description: Evaluate economic repair feasibility based on mechanical damage depth and vehicle residual market value.

rows: Low Coolant / Minor Leak
Hose replacement, expansion tank cap, top-up
Always economical—simple routine maintenance.
Stuck Thermostat
Thermostat housing and seal replacement
Always replace immediately to prevent catastrophic warping.
Failed Water Pump
Water pump replacement + fresh coolant flush
Critical priority; upgrade plastic impellers to metal.
Failed Cooling Fan Assembly
Electric fan motor, resistor pack, or relay
Mandatory if fan does not spin when warm or A/C is activated.
Blown Head Gasket (Flat Head)
Gasket replacement + light cylinder head skim
Viable on vehicles with market value exceeding £2,000–£3,000.
Warped / Cracked Cylinder Head
Reconditioned or new cylinder head assembly
Viable on vehicles worth £4,000+; otherwise consider recon engine.
Complete Engine Seizure
Reconditioned engine replacement
Viable on vehicles worth £6,000+; otherwise salvage vehicle.

Head gasket or cylinder head replacement justified
Vehicle value easily justifies major mechanical overhauls.
Any repair, including reconditioned engine replacement
Warranty coverage and asset protection make full replacement optimal.

blocks.text: The 60% Economic Rule: If the lowest viable repair quote exceeds approximately 60% of current private resale market value, evaluate salvage and part-exchange options before approving workshop teardown.

items.title: Consequences of Delay: How Bad Can It Get?
items.description: Visualising the exponential cost increase of driving with an unaddressed overheating fault.

rows: Stage 1: Warning Signs
Temperature gauge rises intermittently; thermostat sticking or minor leak.
Stage 2: Single Red Event
Engine enters red zone once; cylinder head expands and gasket begins failing.
Stage 3: Repeated Overheating
Cylinder head warps permanently; aluminium anneals and loses structural hardness.
Stage 4: Oil Contamination
Coolant mixes with engine oil; lubrication breakdown destroys crankshaft bearings.
Stage 5: Engine Seizure
Pistons lock solid in bores, cylinder block cracked; scrap metal.

blocks.text: The Cold Hard Maths of Ignoring Overheating: • Fix Immediately Today: £95–£215 (Thermostat replacement) • Ignore for One Week: £550–£1,200 (Blown head gasket + head skim) • Ignore for One Month: £2,500–£6,500+ (Complete engine replacement)

cards.title: What should I do if my engine overheats? +
cards.text: Stop driving immediately. Pull over safely, turn off the engine, and wait at least 30–60 minutes. Do not open the coolant cap while hot as pressurised boiling coolant causes severe burns. Call for vehicle recovery and do not drive again until fully diagnosed.

cards.title: What causes an engine to overheat? +
cards.text: Most common causes: low coolant level due to leaks, thermostat stuck closed, water pump failure (broken impeller), electric cooling fan failure, radiator core blockage, blown cylinder head gasket (consequence of earlier overheating), or critically low engine oil level.
cards.fullText: What causes an engine to overheat? + Most common causes: low coolant level due to leaks, thermostat stuck closed, water pump failure (broken impeller), electric cooling fan failure, radiator core blockage, blown cylinder head gasket (consequence of earlier overheating), or critically low engine oil level.

cards.title: Can I drive with an overheating engine? +
cards.text: No. Driving for even 30 seconds with the temperature gauge in the red zone can warp the cylinder head, costing £600–£1,200 to repair. Continuing to drive until the engine stalls will cause piston seizure and bearing failure, costing £2,500–£6,500+ for replacement.
cards.fullText: Can I drive with an overheating engine? + No. Driving for even 30 seconds with the temperature gauge in the red zone can warp the cylinder head, costing £600–£1,200 to repair. cards.title: How do I know if my head gasket is blown after overheating? +
cards.text: Common signs include: white steam/smoke from the exhaust (burning coolant), creamy mayonnaise-like sludge on the oil filler cap or dipstick, violent coolant bubbling in the expansion tank, rapid coolant loss with no external puddles, and engine misfiring. A garage chemical sniffer test confirms combustion gases (£50–£150 diagnostic).

A garage chemical sniffer test confirms combustion gases (£50–£150 diagnostic).

cards.title: Is a head gasket repair worth it on an old car? +
cards.text: If your car is worth £2,000–£4,000 and otherwise mechanically sound, a £600–£1,200 head gasket repair is usually economical compared to buying a replacement vehicle. If your car is worth under £2,000 and the cylinder head is warped or cracked (£1,200–£3,500), evaluate scrap value first. → Compare repair vs replacement
